title: Studying in Türkiye and Hungary: affordable options
summary: What the Türkiye Scholarships and Stipendium Hungaricum programmes are, how self-financed places differ, and how to compare the two countries on language, cost and documents.

sources.title: Study in Hungary: official information site

review_note: Verified on the fetched official Türkiye Scholarships page: support categories (monthly stipend, accommodation, health insurance, language course, flight ticket and others); no figures or dates on that page. The Study in Hungary site returned a maintenance notice, and the Stipendium Hungaricum site showed a certificate error, so no Hungarian benefits, fees or dates are stated. Turkish public-university fees and any Turkish fee table were not verified and are not stated.
body:
## In short

- Türkiye and Hungary both have state-funded scholarship routes and lower-cost public university places for international students. Both need careful checking, because the rules differ by programme and by intake.
- The Türkiye Scholarships programme is run by the Presidency for Turks Abroad and Related Communities (YTB). Its official site lists the support categories, including a monthly stipend, accommodation, health insurance, a language course and a flight ticket.
- Hungary's Stipendium Hungaricum is the main state scholarship. Self-financed places are a separate route with their own fees.
- Verify every figure on the official site for the year you apply, and never rely on a fee table from an old blog post.

## Türkiye: what the scholarship covers

The official Türkiye Scholarships site lists these support categories: monthly stipend, accommodation, health insurance, language course, flight ticket, and in some categories an academy or diploma component and adaptation support. The site presents the programme as covering both financial support and university placement. Confirm the exact benefits for your category on the site, because a category may cover some items and not others.

The application calendar is published on the official site. Third-party guides sometimes give dates for the next cycle, but those are not confirmed until the official calendar is published, so check the calendar before you plan your application.

## Türkiye: language and the first year

Many Turkish bachelor's programmes are taught in Turkish. If your programme is in Turkish, expect a language stage. Some scholarship categories include a language course before the degree starts. Read your offer letter closely to see whether the language year is included, how long it lasts and what happens if you do not reach the required level.

## Türkiye: university fees

Public universities in Türkiye generally charge much lower tuition than many Western European universities, and some programmes for international students are free. Private universities charge higher fees. Check each university's international admissions page for the current fee table, and note whether the figure is per year or per semester.

## Hungary: Stipendium Hungaricum

Stipendium Hungaricum is the Hungarian government scholarship programme for international students. It funds places at Hungarian higher education institutions and sets the benefits for each intake in its programme rules. Read the programme's official rules for the year you apply, including eligibility, the application route and the benefits that apply to your level of study.

The programme is one of the main ways that students from Central Asia consider Hungary. Compare it with a self-financed place before you decide, since the eligibility, the timing and the costs are different.

## Hungary: self-financed places

Self-financed places at Hungarian universities charge tuition for international students. Fees differ between universities and programmes, and medicine and some other programmes usually cost more. The official study-in-Hungary information site is the place to check current guidance. If the site is temporarily unavailable when you look, check again later rather than using an older number from another source.

## Living costs in both countries

Living costs in Türkiye and Hungary are generally lower than in Western Europe, but they vary by city. Istanbul and Budapest cost more than smaller university towns. Make a budget for your chosen city, using rent in a shared flat, food, transport, phone and health insurance.

Scholarship benefits can cover a large part of these costs, but check whether they are paid monthly, when they start, and whether accommodation is included.

## Documents and recognition

Both countries ask for school certificates to be translated and, in many cases, legalised or apostilled. Check the requirements for your home country and ask the university early, because processing can take weeks. Ask whether your certificate needs to be recognised by the national education authority in the country you are applying to.

## Choosing between the two

Compare these points side by side:

- Language of instruction and whether a language year is needed.
- Benefits in the official scholarship rules, not in summaries.
- Tuition for self-financed places, if you cannot get a scholarship.
- Living costs in the city where the university is.
- Visa and residence requirements and how long they take.
- Your career plans, and whether the degree is recognised in the country you want to work in.

## Common mistakes

- Trusting an older programme calendar or benefit table.
- Assuming a scholarship covers everything when the official list is shorter.
- Missing the language requirement for a Turkish-taught programme.
- Forgetting that a private university has different fees.
- Applying without checking whether your school certificate needs legalisation.

## Choosing a city

Both countries have university towns with lower living costs than the capital cities. A smaller city often means cheaper rent, but it may have fewer jobs, fewer international students and fewer transport options. Visit the university's website to see its international office, its student clubs and its accommodation options. A city that offers good services for international students can make the first year much easier.

## Accommodation

Ask the university whether it offers dormitory places for international students, and how they are allocated. Dormitory rules, deposits and application deadlines differ by university. If you rent privately, check the contract and ask an international office or a local student group to help you review it. Keep copies of the contract, your deposit receipt and any inventory list.

## Language support

Turkish and Hungarian are both demanding languages for speakers of Russian, Uzbek or Kazakh, though many students from Central Asia find that common vocabulary helps. Universities often provide intensive language courses, and some programmes teach part of the course in English. Ask what language support is included, whether it is free, and whether you can take it before the degree begins.

## Health and insurance

Health insurance is important for every international student in both countries. Ask the university which policy it recommends, and check whether the scholarship includes health insurance. Keep the policy card and the provider's emergency number with your documents.

## Staying in touch with family and home

Many students find the first year lonely. Joining a student association, a language exchange or a religious or cultural group can help. Keep regular contact with family and keep your documents in digital form as well as on paper. Plan one trip home or one visit from family in your first year if the budget allows, and check the travel times and costs in advance.

## After graduation

Think early about where you want to work. Check whether the degree is recognised in your home country, and whether you will need to register it with a national body. Ask the university's career office what internships, research jobs and graduate programmes it offers, and whether the Turkish or Hungarian language skills you gain will help you in your target market.

## Checklist

- [ ] Read the official scholarship benefits for your category and level.
- [ ] Check the current application calendar on the official site.
- [ ] Confirm whether your programme is taught in Turkish, Hungarian or English.
- [ ] Check the language requirement and any language year.
- [ ] Look up the current tuition for the self-financed route, if you are considering it.
- [ ] Estimate living costs for the specific city.
- [ ] Start the translation and legalisation process early.
